R Workshop 2: Data Cleaning with dplyr and Plotting with ggplot2

UBC MFRE, Introduction to R

1 R Workshop 2

1.1 How to read this document

Every grey box below is a code chunk: R code that actually runs when this document is knitted. The white box underneath it is the output that R produced. The text around them tells you what the code does, why it is written that way, and how to read the output.

Three habits will serve you for the whole workshop:

  1. Run a chunk, then look at the output before moving on. R is an interactive language. Guessing what a line did is slower than checking.
  2. When a line is unfamiliar, take it apart from the inside out. mean(x) is a function called mean applied to an argument x.
  3. If something breaks, read the error message from the bottom up. R usually names the function that failed.

Some vocabulary that the rest of the document assumes:

  • An object is a named thing stored in memory. x <- 5 creates an object called x. The <- is the assignment operator; = also works in most places, but R programmers use <- for assignment by convention.
  • A function is a named piece of code that takes inputs and returns an output. sqrt(16) returns 4.
  • An argument is one of those inputs. Arguments can be given by position (round(3.14159, 2)) or by name (round(3.14159, digits = 2)). Naming them is slower to type and much easier to read six months later.
  • A package is a bundle of functions written by somebody else. You install it once, then load it in every session where you want it.

Today, we’ll be continuing our dive into R skills. More specifically, we’ll be moving from general ideas (base R work, approaches to coding) to specific software packages we’re importing from others. Specifically, this will be a look into using the Tidyverse library’s dplyr and ggplot2 packages.

The Workshop 1 material was about the language itself: how R stores values, how loops and conditions work, and how to lay out a script so another person can read it. That material is base R, meaning it ships with R and needs no packages.

Sections 3 and 4 are different in kind. dplyr and ggplot2 are packages. They do not add anything R could not already do; they add a consistent vocabulary for doing it. In base R, keeping the rows of a data frame df where column Food exceeds 100 looks like df[df$Food > 100, ]. In dplyr it is filter(df, Food > 100). The second is a few characters longer and far easier to read, and once you know the pattern it transfers to every other verb in the package.

1.3 3. Introduction to Data Cleaning: Dplyr and the Tidyverse

1.3.1 3.1 What is the Tidyverse?

R ships with a few thousand functions. Everything else lives in packages that other people wrote and published. A package has to be installed once per machine (it downloads files onto your hard drive) and loaded once per R session (it makes its functions visible to your code).

install.packages("dplyr") installs. library(dplyr) loads. Running library() on a package you never installed is an error; running install.packages() every time you knit is slow and rude to the mirror server. pacman::p_load() folds the two into one call: it checks whether each package is already installed, installs the missing ones, then loads all of them.

The :: in pacman::p_load means “the p_load function from the pacman package”. Writing it that way lets you call a function without loading the whole package, and it makes the source of the function obvious to a reader.

# p_load() installs a package only if it is missing, then loads it.
pacman::p_load(tidyverse, here, skimr)

Three things arrived in that one line:

  • tidyverse is a meta-package. Loading it loads dplyr (data manipulation), ggplot2 (plots), readr (reading files), tibble (a modern data frame), tidyr (reshaping), stringr (text), forcats (factors) and purrr (iteration). The startup message lists them, and it also lists conflicts: dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter(), so from here on a plain filter() means the dplyr one.
  • here builds file paths that work no matter which sub-folder you are sitting in. Section 3.2 uses it.
  • skimr produces a compact summary of a whole data frame.

The “Tidyverse” is a collection of R packages designed to work together seamlessly and follow a consistent set of principles for data manipulation and analysis. It provides a cohesive and powerful toolkit for data cleaning, transformation, visualization, and modeling, and is the “industry standard” for many data operations in R.

Dplyr is one of the core packages within the Tidyverse. It offers a simple, consistent approach to doing all your basic data tidying operations.

The shared principle worth naming now is tidy data. A table is tidy when

  1. each row is one observation,
  2. each column is one variable,
  3. each cell is one value.

Our CPI file is not tidy when it arrives: the years run across the top as column headers, so a single row mixes 23 different observations. Section 3.2 fixes that, and the fix is most of the reason that import chunk is so long.

1.3.2 3.2 5+1 functions

The “80/20” rule applies in many contexts; that 80% of effects come from 20% of causes.

Example: 80% of my productivity comes from 20% of my working time!

In Dplyr, there’s a similar dynamic with the following functions, perhaps even more extreme: 90% of your data cleaning can be covered by the following 5+1 functions:

  • select()
  • mutate()
  • filter()
  • arrange()
  • summarise()

and,

  • group_by()

The first five do various operations, such as subsetting and altering your data. group_by() is separated, because while it’s almost never used alone, it augments the other functions and adds a whole new dimension of use.

All six share one contract. Learning it once saves you from six separate sets of rules:

  • The first argument is always a data frame. That is what makes them chainable with the pipe in Section 3.6.
  • Later arguments refer to column names without quotes. Inside filter(food_cpi, Food > 100), the bare word Food means “the column called Food in food_cpi”. Outside the function, typing Food on its own is an error, because no object of that name exists in your workspace. This behavior is called data masking, and it is the most common source of confusion for people arriving from Python.
  • They return a new data frame and never modify the one you passed in. That is worth demonstrating rather than asserting, which we do as soon as the data is loaded.

Before we get to the commands themselves, we need to import our data. I’ll set this up in one cell; a few of these commands will be seen again later.

The next chunk re-loads four packages that tidyverse already loaded above. It is redundant, and it is harmless: loading a package a second time does nothing. It is kept because it documents which package each function in the import chunk comes from - read_csv from readr, here from here, mutate and rename from dplyr, as_tibble from tibble.

library(readr)
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

The import chunk transposes the raw file. Transposing means flipping rows and columns, and it is easier to see on a table small enough to print whole:

# A toy table in the same shape as the raw CPI file: one row per product group,
# one column per year. Backticks are needed around names that start with a
# digit, because 2000 on its own is a number, not a name.
transpose_demo <- tibble(
  group  = c("A", "B"),
  `2000` = c(1, 2),
  `2001` = c(3, 4)
)

transpose_demo
## # A tibble: 2 × 3
##   group `2000` `2001`
##   <chr>  <dbl>  <dbl>
## 1 A          1      3
## 2 B          2      4
# t() is base R's transpose. Rows become columns, columns become rows.
t(transpose_demo)
##       [,1] [,2]
## group "A"  "B" 
## 2000  "1"  "2" 
## 2001  "3"  "4"

Two things to notice in the transposed output. First, the year labels 2000 and 2001 are no longer column names; they have become row names, printed down the left edge. Second, every value is now in quotation marks. t() returns a matrix, and a matrix holds exactly one type of value throughout. Mixing the text "A" with the number 1 forces the whole thing to text. Both facts drive the code in the import chunk: it has to recover the years from the row names, and it has to convert the numbers back from text.

Two lines in the import chunk use %>%, the pipe. Section 3.6 covers it properly. For now, read x %>% f(y) as f(x, y): the thing on the left becomes the first argument of the function on the right. So cpi_t %>% mutate(Year = year_col) is the same call as mutate(cpi_t, Year = year_col).

Now the real import. Read it once top to bottom, then read the commentary that follows it.

# The shared data folder sits at the top level of the repository. here() anchors
# on the R project file, so build the path from there. The fallback covers the
# case where the project is opened at the repository root instead of at r/.
data_dir <- here("..", "data")
if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) data_dir <- here("data")

# read csv file in as data
cpi <- readr::read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "food_cpi.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# transpose
cpi_t <- t(cpi)

# assign first row as column names
colnames(cpi_t) <- as.character(cpi_t[1, ])

# remove first row from dataframe
cpi_t <- cpi_t[-1, ]

# get index as year column
year_col <- row.names(cpi_t)

# turn cpi_t to tibble datatype
cpi_t <- as_tibble(cpi_t)

# replace years
cpi_t <- cpi_t %>%
  mutate(Year = year_col)

# rename columns
cpi_t <- rename(cpi_t, "Energy" = "Energy 7", "Food" = "Food 5", "Goods" = "Goods 8", "Shelter" = "Shelter 6", "Services" = "Services 9", 
                "All_items" = "All-items",
                "Household_operations_furniture_equipment" = "Household operations, furnishings and equipment",
                "All_items_but_food_energy" = "All-items excluding food and energy 7",
                "All_items_excluding_energy" = "All-items excluding energy 7",
                "Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis" = "Alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and recreational cannabis",
                "Recreation_education_books" = "Recreation, education and reading",
                "Clothing_and_footwear" = "Clothing and footwear",
                "Health_personal_care" = "Health and personal care")

colnames(cpi_t)
##  [1] "All_items"                               
##  [2] "Food"                                    
##  [3] "Shelter"                                 
##  [4] "Household_operations_furniture_equipment"
##  [5] "Clothing_and_footwear"                   
##  [6] "Transportation"                          
##  [7] "Gasoline"                                
##  [8] "Health_personal_care"                    
##  [9] "Recreation_education_books"              
## [10] "Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis"                
## [11] "All_items_but_food_energy"               
## [12] "All_items_excluding_energy"              
## [13] "Energy"                                  
## [14] "Goods"                                   
## [15] "Services"                                
## [16] "Year"
cpi_t <- cpi_t %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric))

cpi_t
## # A tibble: 23 × 16
##    All_items  Food Shelter Household_operations_furnitur…¹ Clothing_and_footwear
##        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>                           <dbl>                 <dbl>
##  1      95.4  93.3    95.6                            96.7                 100. 
##  2      97.8  97.4    99.1                            98.6                 101. 
##  3     100   100     100                             100                   100  
##  4     103.  102.    103.                            101.                   98.2
##  5     105.  104.    106.                            101.                   98  
##  6     107   106.    109.                            102.                   97.6
##  7     109.  109.    113.                            102.                   95.8
##  8     112.  112.    117.                            103.                   95.7
##  9     114.  116.    122                             105.                   93.8
## 10     114.  121.    122.                            107.                   93.4
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​Household_operations_furniture_equipment
## # ℹ 11 more variables: Transportation <dbl>, Gasoline <dbl>,
## #   Health_personal_care <dbl>, Recreation_education_books <dbl>,
## #   Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis <dbl>, All_items_but_food_energy <dbl>,
## #   All_items_excluding_energy <dbl>, Energy <dbl>, Goods <dbl>,

1.3.2.1 Walking through the import

The path. here() builds an absolute file path starting from the root of your project. It finds that root by walking up from the current folder until it sees a marker file. In this repository the marker is r/r.Rproj, so here() resolves to the r folder, and here("..", "data") resolves to the data folder next to it at the repository top level. The ".." means “go up one level”, exactly as in a file explorer.

The if (!dir.exists(data_dir)) line is a guard. dir.exists() returns TRUE or FALSE, and ! flips it. The sentence reads: if that folder is not there, use here("data") instead, which is the right answer when somebody opens the project at the repository root rather than at r/. Path problems are the most common reason a classmate’s notebook fails to run on your machine. Never write read_csv("C:/Users/yourname/Desktop/food_cpi.csv"). That path exists on exactly one computer in the world.

file.path() glues folder and file names together with the right separator for your operating system, which is why it beats pasting a "/" in yourself.

Reading. read_csv() is readr’s CSV reader. It returns a tibble: a data frame with better printing and no surprise type conversions. The show_col_types = FALSE argument suppresses the block of text that otherwise reports every column’s guessed type. We suppress it only because the data gets restructured immediately.

Transposing. t(cpi) gives a character matrix, exactly as in the toy example. Here is the raw file’s shape before the flip:

# First four columns of the raw import: product groups down the side, years
# across the top. This is the untidy layout described in Section 3.1.
cpi[, 1:4]
## # A tibble: 15 × 4
##    `Products and product groups 5`                          `2000` `2001` `2002`
##    <chr>                                                     <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
##  1 All-items                                                  95.4   97.8    100
##  2 Food 5                                                     93.3   97.4    100
##  3 Shelter 6                                                  95.6   99.1    100
##  4 Household operations, furnishings and equipment            96.7   98.6    100
##  5 Clothing and footwear                                     100.   101.     100
##  6 Transportation                                             97.2   97.3    100
##  7 Gasoline                                                  104.   101.     100
##  8 Health and personal care                                   97     98.9    100
##  9 Recreation, education and reading                          97     98.4    100
## 10 Alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and recreational …   79     85      100
## 11 All-items excluding food and energy 7                      95.5   97.3    100
## 12 All-items excluding energy 7                               95     97.3    100
## 13 Energy 7                                                   98.8  102      100
## 14 Goods 8                                                    96     98.4    100
## 15 Services 9                                                 94.8   97.1    100

Each row is a product group and each column is a year, so one row holds 23 separate observations. After t(), each row is a year and each column is a product group, which is what we want.

Recovering the header. cpi_t[1, ] is the first row of the matrix, which after transposing holds the product-group names. Square brackets are R’s subsetting operator, and inside them the order is always [rows, columns]; leaving one side blank means “all of them”. colnames(cpi_t) <- ... writes those names onto the matrix, and cpi_t <- cpi_t[-1, ] then deletes that row. A negative index in R means “everything except this”, not “count from the end” as it does in Python.

Recovering the years. row.names(cpi_t) pulls the row labels, which are the year strings, into a character vector called year_col. A vector is R’s most basic data structure: an ordered sequence of values that all share one type. A data frame is, underneath, a list of equal-length vectors.

Back to a tibble. as_tibble() converts the matrix into a tibble. Row names are dropped in the process, which is why year_col had to be saved first, and why the next line puts it back as a real column using mutate().

Renaming. The Statistics Canada column names carry footnote markers ("Food 5", "Energy 7") plus spaces and commas. Names like that have to be wrapped in backticks every time you use them. rename() takes pairs in the form new_name = "old_name" and returns a tibble with the names swapped. The bare colnames(cpi_t) line then prints the result so you can check the rename worked before going further.

Fixing the types. Everything is still text at this point, a side effect of t(). mutate(across(everything(), as.numeric)) fixes it. across() applies one function to many columns, everything() selects all of them, and as.numeric converts text to numbers. Note that as.numeric is passed without parentheses: we are handing across() the function itself, not the result of calling it.

Reading the printed tibble at the bottom: the header line says # A tibble: 23 x 16, meaning 23 rows and 16 columns. Under each column name is its type, <dbl> for double-precision numbers. Tibbles print only the first ten rows by default, and the footer names the columns that did not fit on screen.

1.3.2.2 The verbs do not modify your data

This is the point most easily missed, and missing it costs people hours later.

# select() returns a NEW tibble with two columns...
select(cpi_t, Year, Food)
## # A tibble: 23 × 2
##     Year  Food
##    <dbl> <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3
##  2  2001  97.4
##  3  2002 100  
##  4  2003 102. 
##  5  2004 104. 
##  6  2005 106. 
##  7  2006 109. 
##  8  2007 112. 
##  9  2008 116. 
## 10  2009 121. 
## # ℹ 13 more rows
# ...but cpi_t itself is untouched: still 16 columns.
ncol(cpi_t)
## [1] 16

The result of select() was printed and then thrown away, because it was never assigned to anything. cpi_t still has all 16 columns. To keep a result you must assign it: small <- select(cpi_t, Year, Food). Coming from Python, the trap is expecting something like an in-place method. There is none here.

glimpse() is a compact structural summary: one line per column, showing the name, the type, and the first few values. Use it when a data frame is too wide to print.

dplyr::glimpse(cpi_t)
## Rows: 23
## Columns: 16
## $ All_items                                <dbl> 95.4, 97.8, 100.0, 102.8, 104…
## $ Food                                     <dbl> 93.3, 97.4, 100.0, 101.7, 103…
## $ Shelter                                  <dbl> 95.6, 99.1, 100.0, 103.2, 105…
## $ Household_operations_furniture_equipment <dbl> 96.7, 98.6, 100.0, 100.7, 101…
## $ Clothing_and_footwear                    <dbl> 100.3, 100.7, 100.0, 98.2, 98…
## $ Transportation                           <dbl> 97.2, 97.3, 100.0, 105.2, 107…
## $ Gasoline                                 <dbl> 103.5, 100.8, 100.0, 106.4, 1…
## $ Health_personal_care                     <dbl> 97.0, 98.9, 100.0, 101.4, 102…
## $ Recreation_education_books               <dbl> 97.0, 98.4, 100.0, 100.8, 101…
## $ Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis                 <dbl> 79.0, 85.0, 100.0, 110.1, 116…
## $ All_items_but_food_energy                <dbl> 95.5, 97.3, 100.0, 102.5, 103…
## $ All_items_excluding_energy               <dbl> 95.0, 97.3, 100.0, 102.4, 103…
## $ Energy                                   <dbl> 98.8, 102.0, 100.0, 107.9, 11…
## $ Goods                                    <dbl> 96.0, 98.4, 100.0, 101.9, 103…
## $ Services                                 <dbl> 94.8, 97.1, 100.0, 103.6, 105…
## $ Year                                     <dbl> 2000, 2001, 2002, 2003, 2004,…

Read it as a rotated preview. $ Year <dbl> 2000, 2001, 2002, ... says there is a column named Year, it holds doubles, and it starts at 2000. Sixteen lines of output means sixteen columns.

class() and typeof() both describe a column, but they answer different questions. typeof() reports how R stores the value in memory: "double", "integer", "character", "logical", "list". class() reports how R should treat it: "numeric", "character", "factor", "Date". They often agree, and when they disagree the difference is informative. A date has class "Date" and type "double", because R stores dates as a count of days since 1970-01-01.

sapply(df, f) applies the function f to every column of df and returns the answers as a named vector. It is base R’s version of the across() idea.

# Class (factor, character, numeric, Date, etc.)
sapply(cpi_t, class)

##                                "numeric" 
##                                     Food 
##                                "numeric"

# Low-level storage type (integer, double, logical, character, list)
sapply(cpi_t, typeof)

## Household_operations_furniture_equipment

Every column reports class numeric and type double, which confirms the as.numeric conversion reached all 16 columns. Had any column been left as "character", arithmetic on it would fail later with the error “non-numeric argument to binary operator”.

One class you will meet constantly, and that is absent here: a factor is R’s type for a categorical variable with a fixed set of allowed values, called its levels. Underneath, a factor is stored as integer codes plus a lookup table of labels, which is why class() says "factor" while typeof() says "integer". Factors matter because ggplot2 uses level order to decide the order of bars and legend entries, and because regression functions turn factors into dummy variables automatically. We build one in Section 3.6.

Read n_missing first (zero everywhere here, so nothing is missing yet) and complete_rate next (1.00, the same fact as a proportion). After that, p0 and p100 are the minimum and maximum and p50 is the median. Compare Gasoline with Clothing_and_footwear: gasoline runs from about 100 to 247 across the sample while clothing barely moves and spends most of the period below its 2002 base of 100. That spread is why economists rarely quote a single inflation number without saying which basket it refers to.

1.3.3 3.3 select()

select() is conceptually the simplest, and a good place to start for our data cleaning. It is also probably the simplest: you pass in a dataframe, and name the columns you want to keep. It returns just those columns.

As you can see, cpi_t has a lot of non-food columns. We don’t want those. We’ll select just "Year", "Food", and "All_items_but_food_energy" (the names we assigned in the import chunk above), leaving out the others, calling this food_cpi

The generic R function colnames() is useful here, in case we need to alter our selection.

Column names can be given bare (Year) or quoted ("Year"). Both work in select(). Bare names are the tidyverse convention; quotes are needed only when a name contains spaces or starts with a digit, and even then backticks are the usual choice. The code below uses quotes, which is perfectly valid and slightly more defensive.

colnames(cpi_t)
##  [1] "All_items"
