1.3.4 3.4 mutate()

The mutate() function is a tool for performing calculations or transformations on data within a dataframe. You can create new columns based on existing data or modify existing columns, enabling you to process your data for further analysis.

Our datasets contain the Consumer Price Indices for various types of goods. To transform these into inflation percentages, we’ll need to subtract the previous year’s value, then divide by it.

The lag() function is used with a data column: you input this column, and it moves each entry “down” one row. Our data goes from 2000 onwards, so the 2000 value is moved to 2001, 2001 to 2002, etc. The first year doesn’t have a prior value, so this is filled with an NA.

NA is R’s marker for a missing value. It is not zero and not an empty string. Any arithmetic involving NA returns NA, which is the correct and honest answer: if you do not know last year’s price, you cannot know this year’s growth rate.

Before the calculation, look at what lag() actually does. The chunk below builds a two-column comparison and plots both series.

# select() keeps Year and Food; mutate() adds the shifted copy next to it.
lag_demo <- food_cpi %>%
  select(Year, Food) %>%
  mutate(Food_lagged = lag(Food))

# head() prints the first n rows. The 2000 row shows the NA that lag() creates.
head(lag_demo, 4)
## # A tibble: 4 × 3
##    Year  Food Food_lagged
##   <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>
## 1  2000  93.3        NA  
## 2  2001  97.4        93.3
## 3  2002 100          97.4
## 4  2003 102.        100

Row by row: in 2001 the Food column holds 97.4 and Food_lagged holds 93.3, which is 2000’s value. lag() has not changed any number; it has moved the whole column down by one row and filled the gap at the top with NA.

# pivot_longer() stacks the two columns into one, adding a "series" column that
# records which one each value came from. ggplot2 wants data in this long shape
# when you plot several series with one geom.
lag_demo_long <- lag_demo %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Food, Food_lagged),  # which columns to stack
    names_to  = "series",              # new column holding the old column names
    values_to = "index_value"          # new column holding the values
  )

ggplot(lag_demo_long, aes(x = Year, y = index_value, color = series)) +
  geom_line(na.rm = TRUE) +            # na.rm = TRUE: drop the 2000 NA quietly
  geom_point(size = 1.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0: What lag() does to a column",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "Food CPI (2002 = 100)",
    color = "Series"
  )

The two lines have identical shape; the lagged one is the same curve shifted one year to the right, and it starts in 2001 rather than 2000 because its first value is NA. The vertical distance between the two lines at any year is exactly food_change for that year, which is what the next chunk computes.

food_cpi_mutate <- mutate(food_cpi, 
                          # create change of Food CPI versus lagged period's CPI: difference since last year
                          food_change = Food - lag(Food), 
                          
                          # create percentage Food CPI change: subtract previous CPI then divide by it
                          food_change_percent = 100*(food_change)/lag(Food),
                          
                          
                          # then do change and change percent values for All_items_but_food_energy variable
                          All_items_change = All_items_but_food_energy - lag(All_items_but_food_energy),
                          All_items_change_percent = 100*(All_items_change)/lag(All_items_but_food_energy))

food_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
##  2  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  3  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  4  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  5  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  6  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  7  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  8  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  9  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
## 10  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

The percentage formula deserves a slow reading, because the brackets are doing real work.

food_change_percent = 100 * (food_change) / lag(Food)

  • food_change was created two lines earlier, in the same mutate() call. That is allowed and useful: mutate() evaluates its arguments in order, so a new column can be used by any column defined after it. Written out, food_change is Food - lag(Food), this year’s index minus last year’s.
  • Dividing by lag(Food) makes it a proportion of last year’s level. The denominator is last year, not this year. Using Food as the denominator would be a different and less standard quantity.
  • Multiplying by 100 turns the proportion into percent. The whole expression is read left to right for multiply and divide, so 100 * (food_change) / lag(Food) computes (100 * food_change) / lag(Food), which is the same number as 100 * (food_change / lag(Food)).

Where students go wrong is dropping the brackets around the numerator. Writing 100 * Food - lag(Food) / lag(Food) is valid R and completely wrong: / binds tighter than -, so R computes (100 * Food) - (lag(Food) / lag(Food)), which is 100 times the price index minus 1. Check the magnitude of your first result. An inflation rate of 9000 percent means you lost a bracket.

Reading the output: 2022 shows food_change of 14.0 index points and food_change_percent of 8.89 percent, against an All_items_change_percent of 4.96 percent. That single row drives most of the visual argument in Section 4.

As you can see, mutate() creates new variable columns. You specify a new column name, like we did with food_change, and make it equal to a number, value, or calculation. This can include arithmetic operations, like addition (+), subtraction (-), multiplication (*) and division (/). You can also take exponents, and do a whole range of other operations for other data types.

Sticking to just numeric data as we are, the arithmetic operations give us a solid base to work with.

One more property worth stating plainly: these operations are vectorized. Food - lag(Food) is not a loop over 23 rows that you have to write; R applies the subtraction element by element across both vectors at once and returns a vector of 23 answers. Almost every arithmetic operation in R behaves this way, and code that uses it is both shorter and faster than the equivalent for loop.

1.3.4.0.1 Note:

The variables we created involving a lag() all start with a NA value - for the first period of observation, we don’t have a prior period’s value to pull! As a result, it fetches a NA, and we don’t get _change or _change_percent values for the first row.

In some analyses, you’d drop the first row to have a consistent dataset with full coverage. Since we’re still interested in 2000’s CPI values, we’re going to leave it. However, when we do operations involving these columns, we’ll have to use a special method to tell R to ignore these values.

We’ll cross that bridge when we come to it.

# How many missing values did the lag introduce? One per lagged column.
sum(is.na(food_cpi_mutate$food_change))
## [1] 1
# And what a summary statistic does about it if you say nothing:
mean(food_cpi_mutate$food_change)
## [1] NA

is.na(x) returns TRUE/FALSE for each element, and sum() counts the TRUEs because TRUE counts as 1. One missing value, as expected. The mean() call returns NA, not an error and not a number: R refuses to guess. Section 3.7 shows the fix.

1.3.4.1 Exercise (mutate())

Working with consumables_cpi, calculate the yearly change in Gasoline, Energy, and Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis CPI values, and then the percentage changes, as we did above with food_cpi

# Every new column is defined inside the mutate() call, so the column names on
# the right-hand side are looked up in consumables_cpi.
# Note the bracketing: the numerator must be wrapped before dividing by the lag,
# and the multiplier for a percentage is 100, not 0.1.

consumables_cpi_mutate <- mutate(
  consumables_cpi,

  gasoline_change = Gasoline - lag(Gasoline),
  gasoline_change_percent = 100 * (Gasoline - lag(Gasoline)) / lag(Gasoline),

  a_t_c_change = Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis - lag(Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis),
  a_t_c_change_percent = 100 * (Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis - lag(Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis)) / lag(Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis),

  energy_change = Energy - lag(Energy),
  energy_change_percent = 100 * (Energy - lag(Energy)) / lag(Energy)
)

consumables_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 11
##     Year Gasoline Energy  Food Alcohol_tobacco_cannabis gasoline_change
##    <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>                    <dbl>           <dbl>
##  1  2000     104.   98.8  93.3                      79           NA    
##  2  2001     101.  102    97.4                      85           -2.70 
##  3  2002     100   100   100                       100           -0.800
##  4  2003     106.  108.  102.                      110.           6.40 
##  5  2004     118.  115.  104.                      116           11.2  
##  6  2005     133.  126.  106.                      119.          15    
##  7  2006     140.  133.  109.                      122.           7.20 
##  8  2007     146.  136.  112.                      126.           6.30 
##  9  2008     165.  149.  116.                      128.          18.6  
## 10  2009     136.  129.  121.                      131.         -28.9  
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 5 more variables: gasoline_change_percent <dbl>, a_t_c_change <dbl>,
## #   a_t_c_change_percent <dbl>, energy_change <dbl>,
## #   energy_change_percent <dbl>

This version writes Gasoline - lag(Gasoline) out again in the percentage line rather than reusing gasoline_change. Both styles work. Reusing the earlier column is shorter and keeps the two definitions in sync if you edit one; repeating the expression makes each line readable on its own. Pick one and stay with it inside a single project.

Gasoline is the series to look at here. Its percentage change runs from minus 17.5 percent in 2009 to plus 31.2 percent in 2021, and it changes sign seven times over 22 years. Food never moved more than 8.9 percent in a year and never fell at all. Energy prices are volatile in a way food prices are not, which is part of why Statistics Canada publishes an “excluding food and energy” series in the first place.

You can use the transmute() function to create new variables, and keep only these. Create a new dataframe, real_cpis using transmute. Create the following real price indices: - real_food equal to Food divided by All_items - real_gas equal to Gasoline divided by All_items - real_shelter equal to Shelter divided by All_items - real_energy equal to Energy divided by All_items

Also include the Year column!

real_cpis<-transmute(cpi_t, Year,
                     real_food = Food / All_items,
                     real_gas = Gasoline / All_items,
                     real_shelter = Shelter / All_items,
                     real_energy = Energy/ All_items)

real_cpis
## # A tibble: 23 × 5
##     Year real_food real_gas real_shelter real_energy
##    <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>
##  1  2000     0.978     1.08         1.00        1.04
##  2  2001     0.996     1.03         1.01        1.04
##  3  2002     1         1            1           1   
##  4  2003     0.989     1.04         1.00        1.05
##  5  2004     0.991     1.12         1.01        1.10
##  6  2005     0.994     1.24         1.02        1.18
##  7  2006     0.998     1.28         1.04        1.22
##  8  2007     1.00      1.31         1.05        1.22
##  9  2008     1.01      1.44         1.07        1.31
## 10  2009     1.06      1.19         1.06        1.13
## # ℹ 13 more rows

transmute() is mutate() plus a select() of only the new columns. Year appears in the output because it is listed as a bare column name inside the call; without it, the years would be gone.

Economically, dividing a component index by the all-items index gives a relative price: the price of that good measured in units of the average consumption basket. Both series share the same 2002 base of 100, so every ratio equals exactly 1 in 2002, and a value above 1 means that good has grown more expensive than the basket since then. real_food sits at or just below 1 through 2006, exactly 1 in the 2002 base year, crosses above it in 2007, and reaches 1.13 by 2022, so food has outpaced general inflation over the sample without doing so every single year. real_gas is far more erratic: 1.44 in 2008, back to 1.07 in 2020, then 1.64 in 2022. Relative prices are not trends; they move whenever one component moves faster than the basket, in either direction.

A note on the function itself: transmute() has been superseded in current dplyr, meaning it still works and is not going away, but the documentation now points to mutate(.keep = "none") instead. Both produce the same result here.

1.3.5 3.5 filter()

The filter() function in dplyr lets you extract subsets of data based on specific conditions, allowing you to easily filter rows from a dataframe based on your requirements.

You feed in a dataframe, and a condition to apply to one or more columns. It returns only the rows which meet said requirement. Hence, it’s a filter().

select() has a similar effect, just focused on columns. However, most datasets will have more (sometimes many, many more) rows than columns; naming them individually will rapidly become impractical. Instead, we’ll create “boolean conditions”, logical statements returning TRUE or FALSE. filter() will keep only rows for which this value comes up as TRUE.

The comparison operators that produce those conditions:

Operator Meaning
> greater than
>= greater than or equal to
< less than
<= less than or equal to
== equal to
!= not equal to

The one that catches everybody is ==. A single = is assignment, not comparison. filter(df, Year = 2020) is an error; filter(df, Year == 2020) is the test you meant.

food_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
##  2  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  3  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  4  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  5  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  6  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  7  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  8  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  9  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
## 10  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>
filter(food_cpi_mutate, Food>100.0)
## # A tibble: 20 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2003  102.                      102.      1.70                1.70  
##  2  2004  104.                      104.      2.10                2.06  
##  3  2005  106.                      105.      2.60                2.50  
##  4  2006  109.                      107.      2.5                 2.35  
##  5  2007  112.                      109       2.90                2.66  
##  6  2008  116.                      110.      3.90                3.49  
##  7  2009  121.                      112.      5.7                 4.93  
##  8  2010  123.                      113.      1.70                1.40  
##  9  2011  128.                      115.      4.60                3.74  
## 10  2012  131.                      116.      3.10                2.43  
## 11  2013  132.                      117.      1.60                1.22  
## 12  2014  136.                      119       3.10                2.34  
## 13  2015  140.                      121.      5                   3.69  
## 14  2016  143.                      124.      2.10                1.49  
## 15  2017  143.                      126.      0.1000              0.0701
## 16  2018  145.                      128.      2.60                1.82  
## 17  2019  150.                      130.      4.90                3.37  
## 18  2020  154.                      132       3.5                 2.33  
## 19  2021  158.                      135.      3.80                2.47  
## 20  2022  172.                      142.     14                   8.89  
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

20 of the 23 rows survive. Food > 100 is evaluated once per row, producing a vector of 23 TRUE/FALSE values, and filter() keeps the rows where the answer is TRUE. The three dropped years are 2000, 2001 and 2002, the years before and at the 2002 base of the index.

#compare Food col values which are less than the value of all_items....

filter(food_cpi_mutate, Food<All_items_but_food_energy)
## # A tibble: 3 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
## 2  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
## 3  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

Three rows: 2000, 2003 and 2004. A condition does not have to compare a column to a constant. Here both sides are columns, so the comparison is made row by row. These are the only years in which the food index sat below the food-and-energy-excluded index, and after 2004 food never falls back below it.

food_cpi_mutate$food_change
##  [1]   NA  4.1  2.6  1.7  2.1  2.6  2.5  2.9  3.9  5.7  1.7  4.6  3.1  1.6  3.1
## [16]  5.0  2.1  0.1  2.6  4.9  3.5  3.8 14.0

$ extracts one column as a plain vector, which is why this prints as a run of numbers rather than a table. The leading NA is the 2000 value, and this is a useful habit: when a filter behaves strangely, print the raw column and look for NAs.

Let’s get just the years with a really high increase in food prices, like 4% or more.

high_inflation <- filter(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent > 4.0)
high_inflation
## # A tibble: 3 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
## 2  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## 3  2022 172.                      142.        14                   8.89
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

Three years clear the 4 percent bar: 2001, 2009 and 2022. Note what happened to the 2000 row. Its food_change_percent is NA, so the condition evaluates to NA rather than TRUE or FALSE, and filter() drops any row whose condition is not definitely TRUE. That is a deliberate design choice and a common source of quietly shrinking data frames. If you want to keep the missing rows, say so explicitly with filter(df, is.na(x) | x > 4).

As you can see, filter() works by us passing in a dataframe (food_cpi_mutate), and then naming a column (food_change_percent) as part of a boolean condition. In our case, food_change_percent > 4.0 returns TRUE for all rows where we have a greater than 4% inflation in food prices; filter() then creates a dataframe with just these values in it.

Filtering is easier to trust when you can see which rows went and which stayed. The chunk below labels every row with its fate and then plots all of them.

# case_when() checks conditions in order and returns the value after the ~ for
# the first one that matches. The order matters: the is.na() test has to come
# first, because NA > 4 is NA rather than FALSE and would fall through.
filter_demo <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  mutate(status = case_when(
    is.na(food_change_percent)  ~ "no value (NA)",
    food_change_percent > 4     ~ "kept by filter()",
    TRUE                        ~ "dropped by filter()"
  ))

ggplot(filter_demo, aes(x = Year, y = food_change_percent, fill = status)) +
  # geom_col() draws one bar per row, with height equal to y.
  geom_col(na.rm = TRUE) +
  # The dashed line is the threshold used in the filter() call above.
  geom_hline(yintercept = 4, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0b: Which rows survive filter(food_change_percent > 4)",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "Food CPI change (percent)",
    fill  = "Row status"
  )

Three bars cross the dashed line at 4 percent, and those are exactly the three rows filter() returned: 2001, 2009 and 2022. Every bar below the line was dropped. The year 2000 has no bar at all, because its value is NA and na.rm = TRUE told geom_col() to leave it out rather than warn about it. That missing bar is the visual form of the rule stated above: a row with NA in the filtered column is dropped, not kept.

1.3.5.1 Exercise (filter())

food_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
##  2  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  3  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  4  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  5  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  6  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  7  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  8  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  9  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
## 10  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>
# create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where Food is greater than 100.0
# create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where Food is greater than All_items_but_food_energy
# create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where food_change is less than All_items_change



# now create a DataFrame from `food_cpi_mutate` with just the rows where food_change is greater than 1


# now create a DataFrame where food_change is less than All_items change, AND food_change is greater than 1

# hint! you can input multiple conditions separated by commas

Now you’ve learned how to filter with multiple conditions. By default, filter(df, condition_1, condition_2) returns rows where all conditions are met. So, the conditions all have to evaluate to TRUE.

You can also join conditions with |, meaning OR. As long as one of these evaluates as TRUE, the overall statement will evaluate as TRUE, and you’ll return the row.

The three logical operators, and what they do to a pair of TRUE/FALSE values:

Expression Result
TRUE & TRUE TRUE
TRUE & FALSE FALSE
TRUE \| FALSE TRUE
FALSE \| FALSE FALSE
!TRUE FALSE

& is AND, | is OR, ! is NOT. AND makes a filter stricter and returns fewer rows; OR makes it looser and returns more.

food_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
##  2  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  3  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  4  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  5  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  6  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  7  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  8  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  9  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
## 10  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>
# create the last dataframe again, but using an explicit & symbol between conditions rather than a comma

# hint! Wrap each condition in brackets () to make it easier to read and check


filter(food_cpi_mutate, (food_change < All_items_change) & (food_change > 1))
## # A tibble: 3 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2002  100                       100         2.60                2.67
## 2  2003  102.                      102.        1.70                1.70
## 3  2016  143.                      124.        2.10                1.49
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>
# create a dataframe with the same conditions stated, but joined with | instead

filter(food_cpi_mutate, (food_change < All_items_change) | (food_change > 1))
## # A tibble: 22 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  2  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  3  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  4  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  5  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  6  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  7  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  8  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
##  9  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## 10  2010 123.                      113.         1.70                1.40
## # ℹ 12 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

The contrast is the whole lesson. The & version returns 3 rows: 2002, 2003 and 2016, the only years where food rose more than one index point and still rose by less than the all-items series. The | version returns 22 rows, everything except 2000, because almost every year satisfies at least one of the two conditions and 2000 satisfies neither (both of its inputs are NA).

The brackets around each condition are not required by R, which already gives < and > higher precedence than &. They are there because a reader should not have to remember the precedence table to check your work.

You can link a large number of conditions together. If this was a Mathematical Proof class, I might have you figure out something like "Condition_A | Condition_B & (Condition_C & Condition_D) | Condition_E" where A, B, and E are TRUE while C and D are FALSE.

But this isn’t a Proofs class, so we can enjoy ourselves instead, and move onto the arrange() function.

Two shorthands worth knowing before we leave filter(), because they save brackets in exactly the situations that generate bugs:

# between(x, lo, hi) is equivalent to (x >= lo) & (x <= hi), inclusive at both ends
filter(food_cpi_mutate, between(Year, 2010, 2012))
## # A tibble: 3 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2010  123.                      113.        1.70                1.40
## 2  2011  128.                      115.        4.60                3.74
## 3  2012  131.                      116.        3.10                2.43
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>
# %in% tests membership in a set, and replaces a chain of == joined by |
filter(food_cpi_mutate, Year %in% c(2008, 2009, 2022))
## # A tibble: 3 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2008  116.                      110.        3.90                3.49
## 2  2009  121.                      112.        5.7                 4.93
## 3  2022  172.                      142.       14                   8.89
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

Use between() for a numeric range and %in% for a list of allowed values. Writing Year == 2008 | Year == 2009 | Year == 2022 gives the same three rows and is three times as easy to typo.

1.3.6 3.6 a) arrange()

arrange() is a fairly simple function for reordering a dataset. You feed it a dataframe and one or more columns:

arrange(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent)
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2017  143.                      126.      0.1000              0.0701
##  2  2013  132.                      117.      1.60                1.22  
##  3  2010  123.                      113.      1.70                1.40  
##  4  2016  143.                      124.      2.10                1.49  
##  5  2003  102.                      102.      1.70                1.70  
##  6  2018  145.                      128.      2.60                1.82  
##  7  2004  104.                      104.      2.10                2.06  
##  8  2020  154.                      132       3.5                 2.33  
##  9  2014  136.                      119       3.10                2.34  
## 10  2006  109.                      107.      2.5                 2.35  
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

It returns your dataframe, ordered by the specified column. By default, in Ascending order (lowest to greatest).

NA sorts to the bottom regardless of direction. arrange() is the one verb that does not drop missing values, it parks them at the end. So 2000 is still there, at the very bottom of the object, even though its food_change_percent is unknown. Note that the tibble prints only the first 10 of 23 rows and ends with # i 13 more rows, so you will not see 2000 on screen here. Run tail(arrange(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent)) to bring it into view.

The smallest actual value is 2017 at 0.07 percent, a year in which the food index moved from 142.6 to 142.7. The row order changed; nothing else did. arrange() never adds, removes or alters a value.

By wrapping the column in desc(), you can get Descending order (greatest to lowest).

arrange(food_cpi_mutate, desc(food_change_percent))
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2022 172.                      142.        14                   8.89
##  2  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
##  3  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  4  2011 128.                      115.         4.60                3.74
##  5  2015 140.                      121.         5                   3.69
##  6  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
##  7  2019 150.                      130.         4.90                3.37
##  8  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  9  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
## 10  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

2022 is on top at 8.89 percent, followed by 2009 at 4.93 and 2001 at 4.39. Those are the same three years filter(food_change_percent > 4) returned in Section 3.5, which is a useful cross-check: sorting and filtering should agree with each other.

You can also arrange by multiple columns; it prioritizes by column order. So, arrange(df, col1, col2) will be arranged first in ascending order of col1, but wherever rows have the same col1 value, ties are broken by col2

arrange(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent, food_change)
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2017  143.                      126.      0.1000              0.0701
##  2  2013  132.                      117.      1.60                1.22  
##  3  2010  123.                      113.      1.70                1.40  
##  4  2016  143.                      124.      2.10                1.49  
##  5  2003  102.                      102.      1.70                1.70  
##  6  2018  145.                      128.      2.60                1.82  
##  7  2004  104.                      104.      2.10                2.06  
##  8  2020  154.                      132       3.5                 2.33  
##  9  2014  136.                      119       3.10                2.34  
## 10  2006  109.                      107.      2.5                 2.35  
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

With continuous data such as ours, there are very rarely ties to be broken, so arranging by food_change_percent and food_change works out the same as just arranging by food_change_percent.

Second sort keys earn their keep on categorical data. arrange(df, decade, desc(Food)), once decade exists in Section 3.8, would list the decades in order and put the highest-priced year first inside each one. That is a common way to lay out a results table before exporting it.

1.3.7 3.6 b) Ceci n’est pas une pipe

arrange() combos nicely with slice(). First, arrange a dataframe, then get the top X number of rows by using slice(df, 1:X).

slice() selects rows by position, not by value. 1:5 is R’s way of writing the sequence 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, so slice(df, 1:5) returns the first five rows of whatever it is handed. It has no idea what “top” means; the sorting is what makes the first five rows the top five.

Or better yet, start using %>%, also known as “pipes”. Pipes are a tool that lets you easily chain multiple steps, passing the output of one function to the next step for further analysis.

Pipes do not come in basic R, but are imported with the TidyVerse.

The mechanical rule is short: x %>% f(y) is rewritten by R as f(x, y). The value on the left is inserted as the first argument of the function on the right. That is exactly why every dplyr verb takes a data frame first. The design of the verbs and the design of the pipe are the same decision.

# good syntax

food_cpi_mutate %>%                         # takes food_cpi_mutate and passes it forward:
  arrange(desc(food_change_percent)) %>%    # arranges in descending order by food_change_percent and passes it forward
  slice(1:5)                                # slices to first five results
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2022 172.                      142.        14                   8.89
## 2  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## 3  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
## 4  2011 128.                      115.         4.60                3.74
## 5  2015 140.                      121.         5                   3.69
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

As you see, this starts with a dataframe, then “pipes” it into arrange(desc(food_change_percent)), and then pipes that result into slice(1:5)

Note that neither arrange() nor slice() names a data frame anywhere in that chain. Each one receives it from the pipe. Note also that nothing was assigned, so food_cpi_mutate is unchanged and the five-row result was printed and discarded. To keep it: top_5 <- food_cpi_mutate %>% arrange(...) %>% slice(1:5).

Compare it with

# bad syntax

slice(arrange(food_cpi_mutate, desc(food_change_percent)), 1:5)
## # A tibble: 5 × 7
##    Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##   <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2022 172.                      142.        14                   8.89
## 2  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## 3  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
## 4  2011 128.                      115.         4.60                3.74
## 5  2015 140.                      121.         5                   3.69
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>

Both of these get the same result. But our “good” syntax has a much clearer flow to it, almost like a sentence:

“Take food_cpi_mutate and arrange it in descending order by food_change_percent, and then slice the result from 1 to 5”

Indeed, a major part of why Pipes are useful is that they “read” from top down, left to right. In contrast, wrapping functions reads right-to-left, inside to outside. Imagine pseudocode in either of two cases:

dataframe %>%
  function_1(argument_a) %>%
  function_2(argument_b, argument_c) %>%
  function_3(argument_d)

Compare this to:

function_3(function_2(function_1(dataframe, argument_a), argument_b, argument_c), argument_d)

The second statement is far more difficult to read, particularly with the function arguments added.

There is a practical reason beyond readability. To debug the piped version you delete the last %>% line and re-run, and you see the intermediate result. To debug the nested version you have to count brackets. On a five-step chain, that difference is the difference between finding a bug in ten seconds and in ten minutes.

Three details about pipes that come up constantly:

  • Where the %>% goes. It must end the line, not start the next one. R reads line by line and treats a line that looks complete as complete, so a leading %>% produces a syntax error.
  • The native pipe. Since R 4.1 the language itself has a pipe, written |>, which needs no package. For plain x |> f() calls it behaves the same as %>%, and this document uses %>% throughout because that is what almost all existing tidyverse code uses.
  • Placing the value somewhere other than first. With %>% a dot . stands for the piped value, so x %>% lm(Food ~ Year, data = .) works. You will need this for any function whose first argument is not the data.
# All three lines do the same thing.
nrow(food_cpi_mutate)
## [1] 23
food_cpi_mutate %>% nrow()
## [1] 23
food_cpi_mutate |> nrow()
## [1] 23

The top five years are easier to compare as bars than as a table.

top_5_food <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  arrange(desc(food_change_percent)) %>%
  slice(1:5)

ggplot(top_5_food,
       aes(x = fct_reorder(factor(Year), food_change_percent),
           y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  # coord_flip() swaps the axes so the year labels read horizontally.
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0c: Five largest yearly increases in the food CPI",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "Food CPI change (percent)"
  )

2022 is roughly twice the size of the second-largest year, 2009, and the fourth and fifth bars are almost the same height. A ranked table hides that shape; the bar chart makes it obvious that “top five” here means one extreme year plus four ordinary ones.

The x aesthetic in that plot is worth unpacking, because it is the first factor in this document. Year is numeric, and geom_col() on a numeric x axis draws bars at numeric positions and sorts them by year. We want them sorted by size. factor(Year) converts the years to a categorical variable, whose levels are the allowed categories in the order ggplot2 will draw them; by default that order is alphabetical. fct_reorder(f, x) then reorders the levels of f by the values of x, so the levels run from smallest percentage change to largest, and coord_flip() puts the largest at the top.

An alternative to arrange() %>% slice() for exactly this job:

# slice_max() sorts and slices in one step. n = 5 asks for five rows.
slice_max(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent, n = 5) %>%
  select(Year, food_change_percent)
## # A tibble: 5 × 2
##    Year food_change_percent
##   <dbl>               <dbl>
## 1  2022                8.89
## 2  2009                4.93
## 3  2001                4.39
## 4  2011                3.74
## 5  2015                3.69

Use slice_max() or slice_min() when all you want is the top or bottom few rows; use arrange() when the sorted order of the whole table matters, for instance because you are about to print or export it.

1.3.7.1 Exercise (arrange(), %>%)

# arrange food_cpi_mutate by Year in descending order
# arrange food_cpi_mutate by All_items_change_percent in descending order
# arrange food_mutate_cpi by All_items_change_percent, then slice from 1-10 to get the 10 lowest years

# do this using pipes %>% as shown above
# arrange real_cpis by `real_energy` in descending order, then slice from 1-5 to get the highest 5 years of energy prices

For the third exercise, read the comment carefully: it asks for the 10 lowest years, and arrange() sorts ascending by default, so no desc() is needed. The fourth exercise does want desc(). The point of pairing them is that “slice the first ten” means something different depending on how you sorted.

1.3.8 3.7 summarise()

summarise() is used for making bespoke summary statistics.

You can get a generic set of summary statistics by passing your dataframe into the summary() function, as shown:

summary(food_cpi_mutate)
##       Year           Food       All_items_but_food_energy  food_change    
##  Min.   :2000   Min.   : 93.3   Min.   : 95.5             Min.   : 0.100  
##  1st Qu.:2006   1st Qu.:107.7   1st Qu.:106.1             1st Qu.: 2.200  
##  Median :2011   Median :127.7   Median :114.7             Median : 3.000  
##  Mean   :2011   Mean   :126.7   Mean   :115.6             Mean   : 3.555  
##  3rd Qu.:2016   3rd Qu.:142.7   3rd Qu.:124.5             3rd Qu.: 4.050  
##  Max.   :2022   Max.   :171.5   Max.   :141.8             Max.   :14.000  
##                                                           NA's   :1       
##  food_change_percent All_items_change All_items_change_percent
##  Min.   :0.07013     Min.   :1.000    Min.   :0.8606          
##  1st Qu.:1.88273     1st Qu.:1.425    1st Qu.:1.3177          
##  Median :2.44996     Median :1.800    Median :1.6069          
##  Mean   :2.81959     Mean   :2.105    Mean   :1.8164          
##  3rd Qu.:3.45936     3rd Qu.:2.375    3rd Qu.:1.9514          
##  Max.   :8.88889     Max.   :6.700    Max.   :4.9593          
##  NA's   :1           NA's   :1        NA's   :1

summary() is base R and prints one block per column: minimum, first quartile, median, mean, third quartile, maximum. Two things to read here. In the food_change_percent block the median is 2.45 while the mean is 2.82, so the mean sits above the middle observation, which is the signature of a right skew caused by a few large years. And all four lagged columns carry an extra line, NA's :1, reporting the missing 2000 value. summary() tells you about missing data without being asked. Most other functions do not.

However, you’ll often want to get more specific stats. summary() gives us measures of the values themselves - Min/Max, quantiles, Mean - but nothing related to variance. It’s also just raw data over the whole dataset without grouping.

As we’ll see, summarise() offers us a lot more control over what statistics we calculate.

To use summarise(), you first feed in a dataframe. Then, you tell it how to make the variables you want, and these are returned as a new dataframe. To illustrate:

food_cpi_mutate %>% 
  summarise(mean_Food = mean(Food),
            mean_food_change = mean(food_change),
            sd_Food = sd(Food),
            sd_food_change = sd(food_change))
## # A tibble: 1 × 4
##   mean_Food mean_food_change sd_Food sd_food_change
##       <dbl>            <dbl>   <dbl>          <dbl>
## 1      127.               NA    21.7             NA

The output is a one-row tibble. That is the defining behavior of summarise() and the thing that separates it from mutate(): mutate() returns as many rows as it received, summarise() collapses them to one row per group, and with no grouping the whole table is one group.

The naming works the same way as in mutate(). mean_Food = mean(Food) says “make a column called mean_Food holding the result of mean() applied to the Food column”.

(Notice the NA values in the mean_food_change and sd_food_change columns!)

mean_Food is 126.69 and sd_Food is 21.70, both fine. mean_food_change and sd_food_change are NA, because one of the 23 values fed into them is NA and NA contaminates any arithmetic it touches. R is not broken here; it is refusing to invent a number for the 2000 change.

There’s a whole range of functions you can use here.

There are your more basic, standard statistical measures, some of which turn up in summary():

  • sum(): Calculates the sum of values in a column.
  • min(): Returns the minimum value in a column.
  • max(): Returns the maximum value in a column.
  • median(): Calculates the median of values in a column.
  • sd(): Computes the standard deviation of values in a column.
  • var(): Computes the variance of values in a column.

Then there are the ones more related to the structure and elements of your data:

  • n(): Returns the count or number of rows in a group or the entire dataset.
  • first(): Returns the first value in a column.
  • last(): Returns the last value in a column.
  • n_distinct(): Counts the number of distinct or unique values in a column.
  • quantile(): Calculates specified quantiles of values in a column.
  • length(): Returns the length of a vector or the number of elements in a column.

n() is the odd one out: it takes no arguments at all, because it counts rows rather than reading a column. It only works inside summarise(), mutate() and filter(), where dplyr knows what “the current group” means.

Let’s run a bunch of these.

1.3.8.1 NA Note

I mentioned how our mutate() function involved taking lags, resulting in our first row having NA values in several variables. When we feed these into summary statistic functions, we get problems.

Thankfully, we can tell the functions to ignore these rows, and calculate as though they didn’t exist, with the argument na.rm = TRUE. We do this for all the functions except first() and last(); these two are about what’s literally in the data column, so it makes sense we don’t want to ignore the value!

na.rm stands for “NA remove”, and it is an argument of the statistical function, not of summarise(). It goes inside the inner brackets: mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE), never summarise(..., na.rm = TRUE). The default is FALSE on purpose. Silently dropping missing observations changes the sample you are describing, and R makes you say out loud that you meant to.

# Assuming food_cpi_mutate is your dataframe
food_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 7
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
##  2  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  3  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  4  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  5  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  6  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  7  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  8  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  9  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
## 10  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 2 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>
food_cpi_mutate %>% 
  summarise(mean_inflation = mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            max_inflation = max(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            min_inflation = min(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_inflation = sd(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            var_inflation = var(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE),
            first_inflation = first(food_change_percent),
            last_inflation = last(food_change_percent),
            inflation_25 = quantile(food_change_percent, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
            inflation_50 = quantile(food_change_percent, 0.5, na.rm = TRUE),
            inflation_75 = quantile(food_change_percent, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE))
## # A tibble: 1 × 10
##   mean_inflation max_inflation min_inflation sd_inflation var_inflation
##            <dbl>         <dbl>         <dbl>        <dbl>         <dbl>
## 1           2.82          8.89        0.0701         1.74          3.04
## # ℹ 5 more variables: first_inflation <dbl>, last_inflation <dbl>,
## #   inflation_25 <dbl>, inflation_50 <dbl>, inflation_75 <dbl>

Reading the row: mean food inflation over 2001-2022 is 2.82 percent, with a standard deviation of 1.74. The maximum is 8.89 (2022) and the minimum is 0.07 (2017). Variance is 3.04, which is just the standard deviation squared, so reporting both is redundant.

first_inflation is NA. That is the expected answer and the reason the note above says not to add na.rm = TRUE to it: first() reports what is literally in row 1, and row 1 has no value. last_inflation is 8.89, the 2022 figure, because the rows are still in year order. If you had sorted the tibble first, first() and last() would report something else entirely. They describe row position, not time.

The quartiles are worth a second look. The median is 2.45 and the 75th percentile is 3.46, but the maximum is 8.89. Three quarters of the years sit under 3.5 percent and one year is nearly triple that. Whenever the gap between p75 and the maximum is that large, expect an outlier to dominate any regression you fit later, which is exactly what Section 4.3 shows.

There won’t be an exercise for this section, because we’re going to join summarise() with a function that adds a lot more power.

1.3.9 3.8 group_by()

group_by() divides a DataFrame into “groups” based on having shared values in one or more columns. You can then run summary statistics across these to extract information about how they differ.

group_by() on its own changes nothing you can see; it attaches a label to the data frame saying “treat these rows as belonging together”. The next verb in the chain then does its work once per group instead of once for the whole table. That is the entire idea, and it turns summarise() from a one-row report into a comparison table.

Unfortunately for us, the Year changes every year. All our other variables are continuous, making them highly unlikely to share common values. There’s also not much meaningful information conveyed by two years both having a food_change_percent value of, say, 4.92653414.

So, we’ll quickly create some new variables which do split the data into groups.

The next chunk builds two grouping columns. It also reassigns food_cpi_mutate, so from this point on that object has 9 columns rather than 7. Every later chunk, including the plots in Section 4, depends on decade existing, so run this one before skipping ahead.

# Create 'even_years' column
food_cpi_mutate <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  mutate(even_years = ifelse(Year %% 2 == 0, 1, 0))

# Create 'decade' column
food_cpi_mutate <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  mutate(decade = case_when(
    Year >= 2000 & Year <= 2009 ~ "00s",
    Year >= 2010 & Year <= 2019 ~ "10s",
    Year >= 2020 ~ "20s",
    TRUE ~ "Unknown"
  ))

Three pieces of syntax here.

%% is the modulo operator: it returns the remainder after division. 2022 %% 2 is 0 and 2021 %% 2 is 1, so Year %% 2 == 0 is a TRUE/FALSE test for “even year”.

ifelse(test, yes, no) is a vectorized if-statement. It runs the test on all 23 rows at once and returns yes where the test is TRUE and no where it is FALSE. Here it returns 1 and 0, so even_years ends up numeric rather than logical. Storing a TRUE/FALSE as 1/0 is a habit from Stata and it works, but Year %% 2 == 0 on its own would have given a genuine logical column.

case_when() generalizes ifelse() to more than two outcomes. Each line has the form condition ~ value, and the conditions are tested in order, with the first match winning. The final TRUE ~ "Unknown" is a catch-all: TRUE is always true, so any row that matched nothing above lands there. In this dataset nothing does, since the years run 2000 to 2022, but writing the fallback is good practice. Without it, unmatched rows would silently become NA.

food_cpi_mutate
## # A tibble: 23 × 9
##     Year  Food All_items_but_food_energy food_change food_change_percent
##    <dbl> <dbl>                     <dbl>       <dbl>               <dbl>
##  1  2000  93.3                      95.5       NA                  NA   
##  2  2001  97.4                      97.3        4.10                4.39
##  3  2002 100                       100          2.60                2.67
##  4  2003 102.                      102.         1.70                1.70
##  5  2004 104.                      104.         2.10                2.06
##  6  2005 106.                      105.         2.60                2.50
##  7  2006 109.                      107.         2.5                 2.35
##  8  2007 112.                      109          2.90                2.66
##  9  2008 116.                      110.         3.90                3.49
## 10  2009 121.                      112.         5.7                 4.93
## # ℹ 13 more rows
## # ℹ 4 more variables: All_items_change <dbl>, All_items_change_percent <dbl>,
## #   even_years <dbl>, decade <chr>

The two new columns are at the right-hand end. decade is <chr>, a character column, not a factor. ggplot2 will sort character values alphabetically, which for “00s”, “10s”, “20s” happens to be the correct chronological order. That is luck, not design: had the labels been “2000s” and “90s”, alphabetical order would have put the 1990s last.

Now we can see if our stats varied systematically between even and odd years, and by decade.

# Calculate summary statistics ignoring NA values
food_cpi_mutate %>%
  group_by(even_years) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_Food = mean(Food),
    avg_food_change = mean(food_change, na.rm = TRUE),
    avg_food_change_percent = mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE)
)
## # A tibble: 2 × 4
##   even_years avg_Food avg_food_change avg_food_change_percent
##        <dbl>    <dbl>           <dbl>                   <dbl>
## 1          0     126.            3.36                    2.80
## 2          1     127.            3.75                    2.84

Two rows out, one per value of even_years, and the grouping column is carried into the output automatically so you can tell which row is which. Odd years (even_years = 0) average 2.796 percent food inflation and even years average 2.843 percent. A gap of five hundredths of a percentage point across 22 observations is noise. That is the useful result: the calendar’s parity does not predict inflation, and now you have shown it rather than assumed it.

Note that avg_Food did not need na.rm = TRUE because the Food column has no missing values, while the two lagged columns did. Add the argument where the data requires it, not everywhere out of habit.

One behavior to know about: after group_by() and summarise(), the result may still carry grouping information if you grouped by more than one column, and a message will say so. summarise(..., .groups = "drop") returns a plain ungrouped tibble and silences the message. ungroup() at the end of a chain does the same job.

Grouped means are easier to compare as bars.

decade_means <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  group_by(decade) %>%
  summarise(
    n_years                 = n(),   # rows in this group
    avg_food_change_percent = mean(food_change_percent, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

decade_means
## # A tibble: 3 × 3
##   decade n_years avg_food_change_percent
##   <chr>    <int>                   <dbl>
## 1 00s         10                    2.97
## 2 10s         10                    2.16
## 3 20s          3                    4.56
ggplot(decade_means, aes(x = decade, y = avg_food_change_percent)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  # geom_text() writes the value on top of each bar. vjust = -0.4 nudges the
  # label just above the bar rather than inside it.
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_food_change_percent, 2)), vjust = -0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 0d: Average yearly food CPI change, by decade",
    x     = "Decade",
    y     = "Mean food CPI change (percent)"
  )

The 2010s averaged 2.16 percent, the 2000s 2.97 percent, and the three years of the 2020s in this sample 4.56 percent. Read the n_years column before reading the bars: the 00s and 10s each contain 10 years, the 20s only 3. A mean of three observations, one of which is the 2022 outlier, is not comparable evidence to a mean of ten. Reporting the group size next to the group mean is not optional politeness; it is what stops the reader from over-reading the third bar.

1.3.9.1 Exercise (summarise(), group_by())

Calculate three summary statistics for food_cpi_mutate, and grouping by decade.

Only use na.rm = TRUE if you have to!

Now calculate three more summary statistics for food_cpi_mutate, grouping by decade and even_years

For the second one, think about the group sizes before you interpret anything. Six groups drawn from 23 rows leaves the “20s, odd year” cell with a single observation, and a standard deviation computed on one value is NA.

1.4 4. Introduction to Data Visualization: ggplot2

1.4.1 4.1 Basics of ggplot2

  1. Background

ggplot2 follows the “grammar of graphics” approach to data visualization, breaking graphs down into their separate fundamental parts. These components - your geometric objects, aesthetic mappings, scales, etc - are added or modified individually and directly with ggplot2 functions.

This creates a sequential process to building visualizations, where sophisticated plots can be created with simple components.

The practical consequence is that you build a plot by addition. Every ggplot2 plot is a ggplot() call plus one or more layers, joined with +:

ggplot(data = DATA, mapping = aes(MAPPINGS)) +
  geom_FUNCTION() +
  labs(TITLES AND AXIS NAMES)

Two syntax points before anything else.

The connector is +, not %>%. This trips up everybody at least once. ggplot2 predates the pipe, and its + composes plot layers rather than passing data forward. You can pipe into a ggplot() call (data %>% ggplot(aes(...)) + geom_point()), but inside the plot it is + all the way down.

Like the pipe, the + must end the line. A + at the start of a line is a syntax error, and a missing + is worse, because R will happily run the first part as a complete plot and then evaluate the orphaned geom_ call on its own, producing an error that names the geom rather than the missing operator.

  1. Components of ggplot2
  • ggplot()

This is the function you call to initialize a plot in your R code chunk. You feed in a dataframe or tibble as your data argument, upon which your plot will be based.

On its own, ggplot(data = df) draws an empty grey panel. It has data but no instruction about what to draw or where. Both of those come from the layers.

  • Geometric Objects: geoms

These are what you’re likely most familiar with in data visualization: the lines, bars, points, etc, which actually display your data in visual format. In ggplot2, these are all referred to as geom_ first. Some examples are:

– geom_line(): line plot

– geom_point(): scatter plot

– geom_bar(): bar plot

– geom_smooth(): best fit regression line plot

Geometric objects are added on after your ggplot() call after a + sign. These can be layered on top of one another to get more intricate plots. If you’re plotting a relationship between an x and a Y variable, you could call both geom_point() to show all data points, and then a geom_smooth() to show their best-fit linear relationship.

Some geoms function as direct mappings of a data point’s value into a visual field. For example, geom_point() and geom_line() use these values as coordinates on the X and Y axes. Other geoms run some sort of statistical transformation or calculation and display an object based off of this result. geom_smooth() is an example of this case, where the best-fit line between your X and Y variables is calculated, and then drawn over your dataset.

Two more geoms used below that draw nothing from the data at all: geom_hline(yintercept = 0) draws a horizontal reference line at a value you choose, and geom_vline(xintercept = 2020) draws a vertical one. They take a number rather than a column, because they are annotations, not data.

Layer order is drawing order. A geom_smooth() written after geom_point() draws its band on top of the points; written before, the points sit on top of the band. When two layers overlap, the last one wins.

  • Aesthetic Mapping: aes()

“Aesthetic Mapping” refers to the “mapping”, or relation of variables in the data to visual properties (i.e. Aesthetics) in the graph, such as position, colors, shapes, size, etc. They are defined through the aes() function, which can be assigned globally (to the whole plot) if passed into the initializing ggplot() function, or individually by passing this into the geom_ functions.

To map an aesthetic to a variable, assign the aesthetic (several are listed below) as equal to the variable inside your aes() statement. R will assign Levels (i.e. distinct values of the shape/size/color) to your data points based on their values in the given variable. Some of the core visual effects you can alter with aes() arguments are:

  • shape (to change the appearance of scatter plot points)

  • size (setting the size of your visual objects)

  • color and fill (altering color of the outline and interior of objects respectively)

All of these work with discrete variables; size and color are also compatible with continuous variables.

For example, consider a grocery store’s sales data, which has data on item_category, price, and date. We might build a geom_point() plot, with date on the x-axis, price on the y-axis, and an aes() statement with shape, size, or color equal to item_category to also describe item types.

Some aesthetics can be set manually. In your geom_X() function, but outside of the aes() statement, you might pass color = "blue", to make a line or scatter points a specific color.

That last paragraph states the single most important distinction in ggplot2, so it is worth putting a name to it:

  • Mapping means inside aes(): aes(color = decade) says “let the value of decade decide the color”, so ggplot2 picks colors, builds a scale, and draws a legend.
  • Setting means outside aes(): geom_point(color = "blue") says “make every point blue”, full stop. No scale, no legend.

Put a constant inside aes() and you get the wrong thing but not an error: aes(color = "blue") creates an invisible one-level variable whose single value is the text "blue", and ggplot2 assigns it its first default color, which is red. Figures 3 and 4 below use that behavior deliberately, with scale_color_manual() to fix the colors afterwards, which is a legitimate trick for hand-labeling series.

We’ll see examples of all of these below!

1.4.2 4.2 Line Charts

The first plot maps Year to x and Food to y, and draws one geom_line(). Note the mapping = argument name: it is optional, because mapping is the second argument of ggplot(), but writing it makes the call easier to read. labs() sets the axis names and the title, and every plot you hand in should have all three.

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Food)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Food Price CPI", title = "Fig. 1: Changes in Food Prices over Time")

The food index climbs from 93.3 in 2000 to 171.5 in 2022, and the line is close to straight for the whole period except the final segment, which is much steeper. Nothing else in the plot competes for attention, which is what a single-series line chart is for.

This is a fairly basic, serviceable line chart. Everybody gets what it means; no professor will fail you over it. But we can do more with it, customizing color and adding more lines to show a broad range of data.

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Food)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se=FALSE) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Food Price CPI", title = "Fig 2: Scatter+Regplot of Food Prices over Time")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Two layers share the one aes() from the ggplot() call: the points and the fitted line both use Year and Food. method = "lm" fits an ordinary least squares regression of Food on Year, and se = FALSE turns off the grey confidence band that geom_smooth() draws by default. The message R prints, geom_smooth() using formula = 'y ~ x', is telling you the model it fitted; it is a message, not a warning, and it appears every time unless you name the formula yourself.

The fitted line has a slope of about 3.18 index points per year and an R-squared of 0.985, so a straight line in calendar time explains almost all of the variation. Instead of a lineplot, this visualization shows the individual data points with a geom_point object, and a linear best fit line with geom_smooth. It very starkly shows how food prices jump far off their long-run trend in the final time period, as COVID-era high inflation kicks in.

Quantify that last point rather than eyeballing it: the regression predicts a 2022 food index of 161.6, and the actual value is 171.5. The final point sits about 10 index points above trend, which is the largest gap anywhere in the sample.

ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(aes(x = Year, y = All_items_but_food_energy, color = "All_items_but_food_energy")) +
  geom_line(aes(x = Year, y = Food, color = "Food")) +
  labs(title = "Fig. 3: CPI Price Comparisons Over Time",
       x = "Year", y = "Price") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red"),
                     labels = c("All-items", "Food"),
                     name = "Data Series:")

This plot uses the constant-inside-aes() trick described in Section 4.1. Each geom_line() gets its own aes(), with its own y column and a color set to a quoted label. ggplot2 treats those two labels as the two levels of an invisible categorical variable, and builds a legend from them. scale_color_manual() then takes control of that scale: values assigns the colors, labels rewrites the text shown in the legend, and name titles the legend.

The order matters and is easy to get wrong. values and labels are matched to the levels, which are sorted alphabetically, not to the order the geom_line() calls appear. Here "All_items_but_food_energy" sorts before "Food", so "blue" goes to the all-items series and "red" to food. Swap the two geom_line() lines and the colors do not move; change one of the quoted labels to something starting with “Z” and they do.

All-items falls behind Food starting roughly in 2005, gradually diverging until roughly 2021. Both tick up with much higher inflation than before, but Food does so much more sharply.

Repeating a geom_line() per series works, but it does not scale: five series means five near-identical layers and five chances to typo a column name. The tidyverse answer is to reshape the data into long form first, then draw one layer.

# pivot_longer() turns the two value columns into two rows per year: one column
# says which series the value came from, another holds the value itself.
cpi_long <- food_cpi_mutate %>%
  select(Year, Food, All_items_but_food_energy) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols      = c(Food, All_items_but_food_energy),
    names_to  = "series",
    values_to = "index_value"
  )

# 46 rows now instead of 23: two series times 23 years.
head(cpi_long, 4)
## # A tibble: 4 × 3
##    Year series                    index_value
##   <dbl> <chr>                           <dbl>
## 1  2000 Food                             93.3
## 2  2000 All_items_but_food_energy        95.5
## 3  2001 Food                             97.4
## 4  2001 All_items_but_food_energy        97.3
ggplot(cpi_long, aes(x = Year, y = index_value, color = series)) +
  geom_line() +
  # Naming the values explicitly removes the alphabetical-order trap above.
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("All_items_but_food_energy" = "blue", "Food" = "red"),
    labels = c("All_items_but_food_energy" = "All-items excl. food and energy",
               "Food" = "Food"),
    name   = "Data Series:"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig. 3b: Fig. 3 redrawn from long-format data",
    x     = "Year",
    y     = "CPI (2002 = 100)"
  )

The picture is identical to Figure 3, which is the point: same data, one geom_line() instead of two, and color = series is now a genuine mapping to a real column rather than a trick with quoted constants. Naming the values as "column_value" = "color" pairs also makes the assignment explicit, so alphabetical ordering stops mattering. Use the repeated-geom_line() form for two series when you are in a hurry, and pivot_longer() for anything larger or anything you will have to edit again.

Let’s take a look at their percentage growths over time.

ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = All_items_change_percent, color = "All_items")) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = food_change_percent, color = "Food")) +
  labs(title = "Fig. 4: CPI Percentage Changes Over Time",
       x = "Year", y = "Yearly change (percent)") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "red"),
                     labels = c("All_items", "Food"),
                     name = "Data Series:")
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_line()`).
## Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_line()`).

Same construction as Figure 3, different columns. Both lines start in 2001 rather than 2000, because the 2000 values are NA and geom_line() cannot draw a segment to a missing point.

So, Food has consistently higher percentage changes over most of the 2004+ period. How big are these?

The red line sits above the blue one in 17 of the 22 years. The exceptions are 2002, 2003, 2016, 2017 and 2018. Notice also how much flatter the blue line is: the all-items series stays between 0.86 and 4.96 percent, while food ranges from 0.07 to 8.89.

We can actually pass in a modified value as the y value in our geom_line function. If we subtract All_items_change_percent from food_change_percent, we get the difference in these values (amazing!) which can be plotted directly. Positive values show when food prices are growing faster; negative values show when All Items are growing faster.

Doing arithmetic inside aes() is worth noticing on its own. ggplot2 evaluates the expression against the data frame, so any calculation you could put in mutate() can go straight into the mapping. Do it for a quick look; do it in mutate() when the derived variable is part of the analysis, so it is stored, inspectable and reusable.

ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = food_change_percent - All_items_change_percent), color = "turquoise") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Fig 5. Difference in CPI Percentage Change Over Time",
       x = "Year", y = "Percentage Growth Difference") +
  scale_color_manual(values = "turquoise")
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_line()`).

Here color = "turquoise" sits outside aes(), so it is a setting, not a mapping: the line is turquoise and there is no legend. The scale_color_manual() call on the last line therefore does nothing at all, because no color aesthetic was mapped for it to control. It is harmless, and it is a good illustration of the mapping-versus-setting distinction: a scale function can only modify a scale that exists.

The dashed geom_hline() at zero is doing real work. On a difference plot the zero line is the whole reference frame, and without it the reader has to hunt along the y axis to see which side of nothing a point is on.

The differences in their growth rates (Food minus All items) is also consistently positive, meaning Food inflation consistently outpaces normal inflation.

Read the line against the dashed zero before accepting that. The difference is positive in 17 of the 22 years and negative in five: 2002, 2003, 2016, 2017 and 2018. “Usually positive, and positive in every year since 2019” is what the data supports. The peak is 2022, where food inflation exceeds all-items inflation by 3.93 percentage points.

You could say that Fig. 4 and Fig. 5 are two ways of showing the same data; 5 is a transformation of the data in 4. This reduces the information conveyed by Fig. 5; in a year with an inflation of difference of 2%, we could have Food/All-items inflations of 4% and 2%, or of 100% and 98%!

Does this make Fig. 5 a worse plot than Fig. 4? Not necessarily. It all comes down to what you are trying to visualize. If the important relation is the difference itself, then Fig. 5 is the way to go. By reducing the information it shows, it focuses attention onto what matters most.

1.4.2.1 Exercises (geom_line())

  1. Visualize "Food" and "All_items_but_food_energy" on the Y axis and "Year" on the x-axis. Include a vertical line to show when the COVID period begins.

You can make a vertical line with the geom_vline() function. You specify where it goes with the xintercept argument; make this equal to whatever year is appropriate.

colnames(food_cpi_mutate)
## [1] "Year"                      "Food"                     
## [3] "All_items_but_food_energy" "food_change"              
## [5] "food_change_percent"       "All_items_change"         
## [7] "All_items_change_percent"  "even_years"               
## [9] "decade"
ggplot(data = food_cpi_mutate) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(
    x = Year, y = All_items_but_food_energy,
    color = "All_items_but_food_energy"
  )) +
  geom_line(mapping = aes(x = Year, y = Food, color = "Food")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2020) +
  labs(
    title = "Exercise 1: CPI with Vline",
    x = "Year", y = "CPI"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("blue", "red"),
    labels = c("All-items", "Food"),
    name = "Data Series:"
  )

The vertical line is at 2020 because that is when the pandemic starts, but the break in the series is not there. Both lines carry on at their old slopes through 2020. The all-items line bends upward in 2021 and again in 2022. Food does not bend until 2022: its 2021 increase of 3.8 is smaller than its 2015 and 2019 increases of 5.0 and 4.9, whereas its 2022 increase is 14.0. The figure is a good example of an annotation that is defensible but does not mark what the reader assumes it marks, so say in the caption whether the line is an event date or an estimated break.

For a dashed line instead of solid, add linetype = "dashed" as in Figure 5. Both arguments sit outside aes(), because they are settings.

  1. Use durables_cpi to visualize the CPI of the different product types over time.

Five series, so this is the case where pivot_longer() pays off. The shape to aim for is one row per year per product type, then a single geom_line() with color mapped to the product-type column. durables_cpi gained an avg_durables_cpi column in Exercise 3 below if you run that chunk first, so select the columns you want rather than piping the whole tibble in.

  1. Take services_cpi and durables_cpi. For each, calculate an average of their CPI values using mutate(), or any other method of your choice. Create averaged_cpi by using the bind_cols() function to retrieve these from their respective Tibbles, along with the Year variable from one. Then plot the two series in a line plot, called "Exercise 3: Durable VS Service CPI"

This one is hard. Multiple steps and will require some guidance.

colnames(durables_cpi)
## [1] "Year"                                    
## [2] "Household_operations_furniture_equipment"
## [3] "Clothing_and_footwear"                   
## [4] "Shelter"                                 
## [5] "Transportation"                          
## [6] "Recreation_education_books"
colnames(services_cpi)
## [1] "Year"                 "Health_personal_care" "Services"

The plan below is: add an average column to each tibble, keep only what you need from each, glue them side by side, then plot. bind_cols() joins two data frames column-wise by position, so it assumes both are sorted identically and have the same number of rows. That is true here because both came from cpi_t in the same row order. It would not be true in general, and the safer tool for real work is a join such as left_join(x, y, by = "Year"), which matches on a key instead of trusting the row order.

#colnames(durables_cpi)
#colnames(services_cpi)


# Calculate `avg_durable_cpi`

durables_cpi <- durables_cpi %>% mutate(
  avg_durables_cpi= (Household_operations_furniture_equipment+Clothing_and_footwear+Shelter+Transportation+Recreation_education_books) / 5
)

durables_cpi
