# plotting averaged cpi values

averaged_cpi ends up with three columns: Year, avg_durables_cpi and avg_services_cpi. Only durables_cpi_select kept Year, which is why bind_cols() does not produce a duplicate. Had both kept it, bind_cols() would have renamed the second copy Year...3 rather than failing, which is the kind of silent mess that makes joins the better habit.

Two things to think about before you plot. This average weights each component equally, whereas Statistics Canada weights them by expenditure share, so avg_durables_cpi is not an official aggregate and should not be described as one. And the five durable components are on the same 2002 = 100 base, so averaging them is at least dimensionally sensible; averaging a price index with, say, a dollar value would not be.

1.4.3 4.3 Scatter Plots

Another fundamental type of plot is the Scatter Plot, where we establish X and Y axes and represent data points as dots in their respective locations. This allows us to visualize the distribution of our data along chosen dimensions, and can be extended in ggplot2, with other variables denoted through the size or shape of our scatter points.

You might actually consider a line chart to be a specialized form of a scatter plot, with the points represented and then consecutive points represented with straight lines. Fig. 2 also shows the similar option of adding a linear best-fit line to show the overall statistical relationship, rather than the standard line plot approach. We’ll try this too.

One change from Section 4.2 that is easy to miss: from here on, time is no longer on the x axis. The plots below put one percentage change against another, so each point is a year but the years are not in order along the axis. A scatter plot answers “how do these two variables move together”, not “what happened when”.

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 6: Scatterplot of Food vs Non-Food CPI Changes")
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

R prints a warning here: one row was removed because it contains a missing value. That is 2000, whose lagged columns are NA. The warning is correct behavior and worth leaving visible rather than silencing, because a plot quietly dropping rows is exactly the sort of thing you want to be told about.

About as simply as possible, we get a look at how data points are distributed along the Food and All items but food and energy CPI types. Outliers are not statistically identified, but we do get some idea from visual inspection; a clumping around “normal” inflation levels, with one extreme value at over twice the average inflation value.

Excluding the outlier, the points span 0.86 to 2.77 percent on the x axis and 0.07 to 4.93 percent on the y axis, with most of them packed into the lower left. The lone point at (4.96, 8.89) is 2022, more than three times the mean food inflation of 2.82 percent. Remember which year it is; the rest of this section is largely about what that one point does to a fitted line.

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent, shape = decade)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 7a. Previous with Decade shown via Shape")
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent, size = decade)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 7b. Previous with Decade shown via Size")
## Warning: Using size for a discrete variable is not advised.
## Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent, color = decade)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 7c. Previous with Decade shown via Color")
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

The aes() function called in our initializing ggplot() function lets us set features for the whole plot. These aesthetics can be very useful for conveying more information without using new space, a third dimension, or other complicated features. In Figs 7a-c, we see three different ways, using shape, size, and color.

All three plots contain identical data, mapped to decade three different ways. Note that Figure 7b prints an extra warning that the other two do not: “Using size for a discrete variable is not advised.” ggplot2 is telling you that size is an ordered, quantitative channel. A bigger dot reads as “more of something”, and the reader will try to interpret the ordering. That is fine when the variable really is ordered, as decades happen to be, and misleading for an unordered category like province or product type.

Which of these is the best?

Shape?

Size?

Color?

Judge them on three criteria rather than taste. How many levels can the channel carry before it becomes unreadable? Does the channel imply an order that the variable does not have? And will it survive greyscale printing and the roughly 8 percent of men with red-green color vision deficiency? Apply those to the three figures above and to a hypothetical version with twelve categories instead of three, and the answer usually stops being a matter of opinion.

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + 
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 8a. Food, All-items CPI with Linear Best-Fit Line")
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

This is the same fundamental relationship as before, but now visualized with a best fit line, provided by geom_smooth(). This “best fit” is decided by our familiar linear regression method because we specified method = "lm". Other options are available. geom_smooth() defaults to "auto", which uses an internal selection method:

The grey band around the line is the 95 percent confidence interval for the conditional mean, drawn because se defaults to TRUE here; Figure 2 turned it off with se = FALSE. Where the band is wide, the fitted line is poorly pinned down. It flares out at the right-hand end, which is the plot telling you that the slope is being carried by a single point out there.

The fitted slope is 1.32: a one point rise in all-items inflation comes with a 1.32 point rise in food inflation, and the R-squared is 0.41. Drop 2022 and refit and the slope falls to 0.004 with an R-squared of 0.000004. One observation out of 22 accounts for the entire relationship. That is not a reason to delete the point; it is a reason to report both numbers.

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate, mapping = aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "auto") + 
  labs(x = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
       y = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)",
       title = "Fig 8b. Food, All-items CPI with Local Regression Best-Fit Line")
## `geom_smooth()` using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing non-finite outside the scale range
## (`stat_smooth()`).
## Warning: Removed 1 row containing missing values or values outside the scale range
## (`geom_point()`).

It defaults to "loess", or local regression, a more flexible technique that involves multiple polynomials.

The message R prints confirms it: geom_smooth() using method = 'loess' and formula = 'y ~ x'. The rule geom_smooth() applies is size-based, using loess for fewer than 1000 observations and a generalized additive model above that. So "auto" on a small sample and "auto" on a large one fit different models, and a plot whose method changes when you add data is not a plot you want in a paper. Name the method.

Between Figures 8a and 8b, both are clearly imperfect. Our outlier almost certainly has heavy leverage on the final result. In normal circumstances, defaulting to "lm" is safe and easily explainable, being the direct correlation between your variables rather than a “black box” model decided by R, and so "lm" would be my general recommendation.

The refit above makes “heavy leverage” precise rather than impressionistic. Loess is affected differently: it fits locally, so 2022 bends only the right-hand end of the curve instead of tilting the whole line, which is why the middle of the loess curve is nearly flat while the OLS line slopes.

When one point matters this much, label it. The chunk below draws the same scatter and writes the year next to any point above 4 percent food inflation.

ggplot(food_cpi_mutate,
       aes(x = All_items_change_percent, y = food_change_percent)) +
  geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
  # A geom can take its own data argument. Here only the high-inflation rows are
  # passed to geom_text(), so only those three points get labeled.
  geom_text(
    data    = filter(food_cpi_mutate, food_change_percent > 4),
    mapping = aes(label = Year),
    nudge_y = 0.35,   # move the label up a little so it clears the point
    size    = 3
  ) +
  # formula = y ~ x states the model explicitly and silences the message.
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, formula = y ~ x, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Fig 8c. Fig 8a with the high-inflation years labeled",
    x     = "All-items excl. food and energy: yearly change (percent)",
    y     = "Food CPI: yearly change (percent)"
  )

The three labeled points are 2022, 2009 and 2001, the same three filter() returned in Section 3.5. 2022 sits far up and to the right of everything else, while 2009 and 2001 are high on the y axis but ordinary on the x axis: those were years of high food inflation without high general inflation. 2022 is the only year where both moved together, which is why it alone controls the slope.

Passing data = to a single geom is the general mechanism worth taking away. Layers inherit the plot’s data and mappings by default, and either can be overridden per layer. That is how you annotate a subset, overlay a second data source, or highlight specific observations.

1.4.3.1 Exercises (geom_point() and geom_smooth())

Use food_cpi_mutate for the exercises.

  1. Make a scatterplot with Year on the x-axis, Food on the Y-axis, and a linear trendline. Make sure to give it an appropriate title in the labs() argument!

As we can see, we have a fairly strong fit of our data points to our linear best-fit line; inflation increases prices by a roughly equal amount between most periods.

The regression behind that plot has an R-squared of 0.985 and a slope of 3.18 index points per year, so “fairly strong” is an understatement for the fit and “roughly equal amount” is the right reading of the slope: the index gains about the same number of points each year, not the same percentage.

Note that with inflation being targeted to 2%, this would suggest over longer periods any linear relation in CPI would break down, as the compounding increases cause bigger and bigger gaps. However, this is not a problem on our ~20 year timeline.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly. Constant percentage growth is exponential in levels, so a genuinely constant 2 percent inflation would curve upward on this plot, not run straight. Over 23 years at 2 percent the curvature is too small to see against the year-to-year noise. Over 60 years it would dominate, and the linear fit would be visibly wrong.

  1. Make a scatter plot with food_change_percent on the Y-axis, Year on the x-axis, and a geom_smooth(). For the best fit line, try both "lm" and "loess" and pick whichever you feel works best.

Now, plotting our percentage increases directly, we see that their trajectory is largely flat. They’re mostly distributed around a constant average near 2.8% with random dispersions. As we’ve seen many times, 2022 is a major outlier, and by a proportionally greater amount than in the Exercise 4 plot of price levels.

Numbers for that claim: the mean is 2.82 percent, and regressing food_change_percent on Year gives a slope of 0.036 percentage points per year with an R-squared of 0.018 and a p-value of 0.56. Flat, and not distinguishable from flat.

  1. An interesting point of discussion is how these results fit together. The Exercise 4 plot shows us a roughly constant increase in CPI level; the Exercise 5 plot shows inflation varies year to year, but has no long-run trend in any particular direction. Do these results make sense together? Discuss with your partners, then as a group.

Two things to have straight before you argue about it. A price index and its growth rate are different objects: one is a level, the other is a first difference expressed as a share of the previous level. And “no trend in the growth rate” is a statement about the second derivative of the level series, not the first. Work out what a perfectly constant 2.8 percent inflation rate would produce in the Exercise 4 plot, and what a perfectly constant 3.18 index-points-per-year increase would produce in the Exercise 5 plot, and the question mostly answers itself.

2 Conclusion

During Workshop 1, we went over the basics of R programming, and the methods you should always try to keep in mind, regardless of what you’re doing. Today, we focused on specifics.

In Section 3, we introduced dplyr, a very powerful tool for data cleaning. No matter the project, the data you get will never be fully ready to start running your model. There will always be issues with it, cleaning and transformations that need to be carried out. dplyr gives us many different tools, reaching well beyond the methods I taught today, and I expect you’ll use most of these on any serious empirical project.

In Section 4, we focused on data visualization using ggplot2. Part of the same tidyverse library as dplyr, it allows us to assemble sophisticated and custom-built plots from simple components. This will be useful both in the initial exploration of your data when starting a project, and when displaying your final results.

2.1 What to take away

The six dplyr verbs, and the one sentence that describes each:

Verb What it changes
select() which columns you keep, and their order
mutate() adds columns computed from existing ones
filter() which rows you keep, based on a logical test
arrange() the order of the rows
summarise() collapses many rows into one row of statistics
group_by() makes the verb after it run once per group

All six take a data frame first, return a new data frame, and never modify the original. That is what makes %>% work, and it is why an unassigned result is printed and lost.

For ggplot2, the skeleton is always data, then mappings inside aes(), then one or more geom_ layers joined with +, then labs(). The distinction that causes the most confusion is mapping (inside aes(), driven by a column, produces a legend) versus setting (outside aes(), a fixed value, no legend).

Three habits from today that generalize past this dataset:

  1. Look at the data after every restructuring step. The import chunk in Section 3.2 has eight of them, and a single wrong one produces a table that looks plausible and is wrong.
  2. Handle NA explicitly. The lagged columns carry one, and it changed the behavior of mean(), filter(), geom_line() and geom_point() in four different ways in this document.
  3. Put a number on what a plot appears to show. “Food inflation outpaces general inflation” became “in 17 of 22 years, peaking at a 3.93 point gap in 2022”, and “the outlier has leverage” became “the slope falls from 1.32 to 0.004 without it”. The plot finds the claim; the arithmetic settles it.
